---
title: "About eco"
---

## The question

The [Item Response Warehouse](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org) harmonises
item response data into one long-format table with three required columns,
`id`, `item` and `resp`, so that psychometric methods can be benchmarked at
scale on hundreds of real datasets. Could the same move work for the
hierarchical models ecologists fit with NIMBLE, JAGS and `unmarked`:
occupancy, N-mixture, capture-recapture and community models, where a site
or an animal has a latent state observed imperfectly across repeated surveys?

## Why the structure maps

| Ecology | Latent state per unit | Probe | Item-response analogue |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single-season occupancy | site occupied or not | visit | one dichotomous item, repeated trials |
| N-mixture | site abundance | visit, binomial count | count item, repeated trials |
| Cormack-Jolly-Seber | individual alive at time t | capture session | longitudinal 0/1 item with an absorbing state |
| Dynamic occupancy | site occupied in season t | visit within season | longitudinal item, hidden Markov over waves |
| Community occupancy | site by species | species by visit | multilevel IRT with species as items |

The community occupancy model is the clearest case. The probability of
detecting species k at site i on visit j has a species-level random effect in
its intercept, which is a random-item model. That is what motivates putting
the species, rather than the visit, on `taxon`.

## What the study found

**It round-trips.** Six datasets bundled with R packages, covering
single-season occupancy, N-mixture, removal sampling, CJS, dynamic occupancy
and a 158-species community dataset, convert to the format, validate, convert
back to identical arrays, and give identical model estimates in `unmarked`,
`marked` and NIMBLE on native and reconstructed data. The only things lost are
covariate values at surveys that never happened and units that were never
surveyed, which matter to no likelihood but need a side table if the sampling
frame matters.

**Real deposits behave.** Six public deposits were then built the way the IRW
builds tables. The explicit-zero rule was never ambiguous: every deposit used
blank for "not surveyed" and 0 for "not detected", and in two of them the
pattern could be cross-checked against an effort table. Coarsening was needed
once, for an Endangered tapir deposited with exact camera coordinates. A
multi-state loon table fit with `y` as a species-specific state code. A
MARK input file with losses on capture exercised the `obs_removed` encoding.
One covariate that was really a model output was dropped.

**The data exists and is open.** Dryad alone has on the order of a thousand
hits for the core search terms, nearly all CC0, usually deposited as the very
site-by-occasion matrix the standard targets. A seed corpus of 50 to 100
tables is weeks of work; a harvested corpus of several hundred to a thousand,
most with 20 to 300 units and 2 to 12 occasions, is months. The corpus is one
of small tables, which is where IRW's floor of 100 ids would exclude most of
ecology.

## Five open decisions

These are the design choices the draft takes a position on but does not
settle.

1. **What plays the role of the item?** The draft puts the species on
   `taxon`, so single-species tables look like IRW's repeated-trial family and
   community tables are species-as-items. Putting the visit there instead
   makes every table a person-by-item matrix an IRT model can read directly,
   but does not generalise to multi-species data.
2. **Dense zeros or a surveys table?** The explicit-zero rule makes community
   tables large and repeats observation covariates across species. The
   alternative is Darwin Core's event-core model: a sparse detections table
   plus a surveys table. The draft recommends dense for IRW-likeness and
   self-containment.
3. **The sample floor.** 100 ids is wrong for ecology. The draft proposes at
   least 30 units and at least 2 occasions, but two of the six built tables
   fall below it, and one of those has 10 sites with 43 species and 20 surveys
   each, so a flat unit floor measures the wrong axis for community data.
4. **Sensitive-species coordinates.** Coarsen by rule to a 0.1-degree grid
   with the uncertainty recorded, or drop coordinates for any flagged taxon.
5. **How far to stretch.** Double-observer and binned distance sampling fit by
   using `occasion` for a category rather than a time-ordered replicate;
   spatial capture-recapture adds a `trap` index. Accept the stretched
   semantics with a declared unit kind and response type, or keep
   version 1 to the families where the format is unforced.

## People and code

The project is run by [Ben Domingue](https://github.com/ben-domingue) at
Stanford, as an offshoot of the Item Response Warehouse. The code, the
standard and this site are at
[github.com/ben-domingue/eco](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco). Questions
and claims on candidates go through the repository's issues.
